co-same.1.t0.name: co-same.1.t1.eleven_v3
co-same.1.t0.text: two retirees with the same balance, the same withdrawals and the same average return.

co-broke.1.t0.name: co-broke.1.t1.eleven_v3
co-broke.1.t0.text: One ran out of money in 1991.

a1-start.1.t0.name: a1-start.1.t0.eleven_v3
a1-start.1.t0.text: The first retiree starts with $1 million, measured in 1966 dollars.

a1-start.2.t0.name: a1-start.2.t2.eleven_v3
a1-start.2.t0.text: Their money is the water in this glass tank.

a1-who.1.t0.name: a1-who.1.t2.eleven_multilingual_v2
a1-who.1.t0.text: They retire at the start of a hard decade for markets, though nobody knows it yet.

a1-hook.1.t0.name: a1-hook.1.t0.eleven_v3
a1-hook.1.t0.text: By the end of this video, you will know which 10 years decided the fate of this retiree, and whether the same thing held for every start year since 1928.

a1-mix.1.t0.name: a1-mix.1.t0.eleven_v3
a1-mix.1.t0.text: The money sits in a portfolio of 60 % stocks and 40 % bonds.

a1-assets.1.t0.name: a1-assets.1.t3.eleven_v3
a1-assets.1.t0.text: The stocks are the Standard & Poor's 500 Index, with dividends reinvested.

a1-assets.2.t0.name: a1-assets.2.t2.eleven_v3
a1-assets.2.t0.text: The bonds are 10 -year U .S. Treasury bonds.

a1-rebal.1.t0.name: a1-rebal.1.t2.eleven_v3
a1-rebal.1.t0.text: Every January, the portfolio is rebalanced back to that mix.

a1-rule.1.t0.name: a1-rule.1.t0.eleven_v3
a1-rule.1.t0.text: In the first year, the retiree withdraws 4 % of the starting balance.

a1-raise.1.t0.name: a1-raise.1.t3.eleven_v3
a1-raise.1.t0.text: After that, the withdrawal rises each year with the previous year's inflation. So it always buys the same groceries.

a1-raise.2.t0.name: a1-raise.2.t0.eleven_v3
a1-raise.2.t0.text: The tap is that withdrawal, and it widens as prices rise.

a1-real.1.t0.name: a1-real.1.t2.eleven_multilingual_v2
a1-real.1.t0.text: In real terms, it never changes.

a1-real.2.t0.name: a1-real.2.t3.eleven_v3
a1-real.2.t0.text: In nominal terms, the dollars of the day, it climbs every year.

a1-horizon.1.t0.name: a1-horizon.1.t1.eleven_v3
a1-horizon.1.t0.text: The plan runs for 30 years, from 1966 through 1995.

a1-horizon.2.t0.name: a1-horizon.2.t2.eleven_v3
a1-horizon.2.t0.text: Each stone on this road is one year's return. A losing year sinks below the road.

a1-horizon.3.t0.name: a1-horizon.3.t0.eleven_v3
a1-horizon.3.t0.text: As the tank passes each stone, the water rises or falls with that year.

a1-notax.2.t0.name: a1-notax.2.t1.eleven_v3
a1-notax.2.t0.text: We keep the model this bare on purpose so that one thing can change at a time.

a1-notax.3.t0.name: a1-notax.3.t1.eleven_v3
a1-notax.3.t0.text: The data is U .S. only, and this is history, not a forecast.

a1-mirror-rule.1.t0.name: a1-mirror-rule.1.t2.eleven_v3
a1-mirror-rule.1.t0.text: The Mirror retiree lives through the exact same 30 annual returns, but in reverse order.

a1-mirror-rule.2.t0.name: a1-mirror-rule.2.t0.eleven_v3
a1-mirror-rule.2.t0.text: The return of 1995 arrives first, and the return of 1966 arrives last.

a1-mirror-rule.3.t0.name: a1-mirror-rule.3.t1.eleven_v3
a1-mirror-rule.3.t0.text: So the mirror tank walks the same road the other way.

a1-illus.1.t0.name: a1-illus.1.t1.eleven_v3
a1-illus.1.t0.text: This retiree is illustrative. No one lived through these years in this order.

a1-samewd.1.t0.name: a1-samewd.1.t0.eleven_v3
a1-samewd.1.t0.text: Inflation stays in its real calendar order, so both retirees take out the same dollars every year.

a1-question.1.t0.name: a1-question.1.t1.eleven_v3
a1-question.1.t0.text: Here is the question this first part answers.

a1-question.2.t0.name: a1-question.2.t2.eleven_multilingual_v2
a1-question.2.t0.text: If two people earn the same average return, do they end up in the same place?

a1-avg1966.1.t0.name: a1-avg1966.1.t1.eleven_v3
a1-avg1966.1.t0.text: The portfolio of the 1966 retiree earned an average return of 9 .7%.

a1-avgmirror.1.t0.name: a1-avgmirror.1.t1.eleven_v3
a1-avgmirror.1.t0.text: For the Mirror retiree, the average is also 9 .7%.

a1-geo.1.t0.name: a1-geo.1.t3.eleven_v3
a1-geo.1.t0.text: That is the geometric average, the compound rate that turns the starting dollar into the ending dollar.

a1-geo.2.t0.name: a1-geo.2.t1.eleven_v3
a1-geo.2.t0.text: Multiplication does not care about order. So the same years in any order give the same average.

a1-arith.1.t0.name: a1-arith.1.t2.eleven_v3
a1-arith.1.t0.text: Even the simple arithmetic average, adding up the 30 returns and dividing by 30 is the same for both, 10 .3%.

a1-payoff.4.t0.name: a1-payoff.4.t2.eleven_v3
a1-payoff.4.t0.text: The only thing that differs is the order.

a2-est.1.t0.name: a2-est.1.t2.eleven_v3
a2-est.1.t0.text: Watch the two balances year by year.

a2-q.1.t0.name: a2-q.1.t0.eleven_v3
a2-q.1.t0.text: The question now, when does the order start to matter and how much does it cost?

a2-y1.3.t0.name: a2-y1.3.t0.eleven_v3
a2-y1.3.t0.text: The Mirror retiree gets the 1995 return first, a gain of 31 .7%.

a2-gap1.1.t0.name: a2-gap1.1.t1.eleven_v3
a2-gap1.1.t0.text: One year in, and the paths have already split.

a2-infl.2.t0.name: a2-infl.2.t0.eleven_v3
a2-infl.2.t0.text: By 1969, it is 6 .2 % a year, and every withdrawal grows with it.

a2-7374.1.t0.name: a2-7374.1.t0.eleven_v3
a2-7374.1.t0.text: After inflation, stocks and bonds both lose money in 1973 and 1974.

a2-1974inf.1.t0.name: a2-1974inf.1.t2.eleven_v3
a2-1974inf.1.t0.text: In 1974 alone, the portfolio loses 14 .7%, while prices rise 12 .3%.

a2-bal74.1.t0.name: a2-bal74.1.t3.eleven_v3
a2-bal74.1.t0.text: In 1966 dollars, the 1966 retiree ends 1974 with $461 ,000.

a2-bal74m.1.t0.name: a2-bal74m.1.t1.eleven_multilingual_v2
a2-bal74m.1.t0.text: The Mirror Retiree, same year, same withdrawals, $1 .27 million, also in 1966 dollars.

a2-bite.1.t0.name: a2-bite.1.t2.eleven_v3
a2-bite.1.t0.text: Here is why a bad start is so hard to undo.

a2-bite.2.t0.name: a2-bite.2.t0.eleven_v3
a2-bite.2.t0.text: The withdrawal is still $40 ,000 in 1966 dollars, but it is now taken from a much smaller pile.

a2-sell.1.t0.name: a2-sell.1.t2.eleven_v3
a2-sell.1.t0.text: Every dollar withdrawn after a loss is a dollar that is not there when the recovery comes.

a2-seq.1.t0.name: a2-seq.1.t0.eleven_multilingual_v2
a2-seq.1.t0.text: Analysts call this sequence of returns risk.

a2-7576n.1.t0.name: a2-7576n.1.t2.eleven_v3
a2-7576n.1.t0.text: In 1975, the portfolio gains 23 .6%, and in 1976, another 20 .7%.

a2-7576b.1.t0.name: a2-7576b.1.t3.eleven_v3
a2-7576b.1.t0.text: but they compound on a balance that has already been cut while the withdrawals keep rising.

a2-grind.1.t0.name: a2-grind.1.t0.eleven_v3
a2-grind.1.t0.text: Through the rest of the decade, inflation keeps rising.

a2-1981.1.t0.name: a2-1981.1.t0.eleven_v3
a2-1981.1.t0.text: By 1981, the yearly withdrawal has grown to $108 ,553 in nominal dollars.

a2-1982.1.t0.name: a2-1982.1.t0.eleven_v3
a2-1982.1.t0.text: Then, in 1982, the good years finally arrived.

a2-1982w.1.t0.name: a2-1982w.1.t3.eleven_v3
a2-1982w.1.t0.text: But the withdrawal now takes 16 .9 % of what is left.

a2-mirror-boom.1.t0.name: a2-mirror-boom.1.t0.eleven_v3
a2-mirror-boom.1.t0.text: For the mirror retiree, those same years came first when the balance was largest.

a2-climax.1.t0.name: a2-climax.1.t3.eleven_v3
a2-climax.1.t0.text: In 1966 dollars, the Mirror Retiree is now ahead by 1 .96 million dollars.

a2-years.1.t0.name: a2-years.1.t0.eleven_v3
a2-years.1.t0.text: At $40 ,000 a year in 1966 dollars, that gap would pay for 49 more years of withdrawals.

a2-rest.1.t0.name: a2-rest.1.t2.eleven_v3
a2-rest.1.t0.text: From there, the story of the 1966 retiree is short.

a2-mirror-late.1.t0.name: a2-mirror-late.1.t0.eleven_v3
a2-mirror-late.1.t0.text: The mirror retiree meets the bad years late. The 1974 loss arrives in 1987 on a balance big enough to absorb it.

a2-1991.1.t0.name: a2-1991.1.t3.eleven_v3
a2-1991.1.t0.text: The account pays out its last $96 ,829, in nominal dollars, and hits zero in 1991.

a2-short.1.t0.name: a2-short.1.t2.eleven_multilingual_v2
a2-short.1.t0.text: That last payment is short of the full withdrawal, and the final four years of the plan get nothing.

a2-mirror-end.1.t0.name: a2-mirror-end.1.t3.eleven_v3
a2-mirror-end.1.t0.text: The Mirror Retiree finishes 1995 with $6 .96 million in nominal dollars.

a2-mirror-real.1.t0.name: a2-mirror-real.1.t1.eleven_v3
a2-mirror-real.1.t0.text: In 1966 dollars, that is $1 .44 million, more than the starting balance, after 30 years of withdrawals.

a2-payoff.2.t0.name: a2-payoff.2.t2.eleven_v3
a2-payoff.2.t0.text: The average did not decide who went broke.

a3-all.1.t0.name: a3-all.1.t0.eleven_v3
a3-all.1.t0.text: We ran the same rules for every start year, from 1928 to 1996.

a3-all.2.t0.name: a3-all.2.t2.eleven_v3
a3-all.2.t0.text: That is 69 retirements, each with 30 years of data.

a3-q.1.t0.name: a3-q.1.t0.eleven_v3
a3-q.1.t0.text: The question for this part, what actually decides the outcome?

a3-fine.1.t0.name: a3-fine.1.t0.eleven_v3
a3-fine.1.t0.text: Most of these retirees never ran out.

a3-fine.2.t0.name: a3-fine.2.t0.eleven_v3
a3-fine.2.t0.text: In 65 of the 69 start years, the money lasted all 30 years.

a3-good.1.t0.name: a3-good.1.t3.eleven_v3
a3-good.1.t0.text: A retiree who started in 1982 under the same rules ended with $5 .36 million in 1982 dollars.

a3-1929.1.t0.name: a3-1929.1.t0.eleven_v3
a3-1929.1.t0.text: Even a retiree who started in 1929, the year of the crash, never ran out.

a3-1929.2.t0.name: a3-1929.2.t0.eleven_v3
a3-1929.2.t0.text: Prices fell through the depression, so the withdrawal shrank, and after inflation, the first decade still averaged 3 .9 % a year.

a3-nohurt.1.t0.name: a3-nohurt.1.t1.eleven_v3
a3-nohurt.1.t0.text: For many start years, the order of returns did no harm at all.

a3-less.1.t0.name: a3-less.1.t1.eleven_v3
a3-less.1.t0.text: Surviving is not the same as thriving.

a3-less.2.t0.name: a3-less.2.t3.eleven_v3
a3-less.2.t0.text: In 26 of the 69 start years, the retiree ended with less than the starting balance after inflation.

a3-four.1.t0.name: a3-four.1.t3.eleven_v3
a3-four.1.t0.text: Four start years ran out of money, beginning with 1965 and 1966.

a3-avg-not.1.t0.name: a3-avg-not.1.t1.eleven_v3
a3-avg-not.1.t0.text: Their long run averages, do not single them out.

a3-real66.1.t0.name: a3-real66.1.t3.eleven_v3
a3-real66.1.t0.text: After inflation, the 1966 retiree averaged 4 .1 % a year over all 30 years.

a3-real66.2.t0.name: a3-real66.2.t2.eleven_v3
a3-real66.2.t0.text: 17 start years had a lower real average than that and never ran out.

a3-1969.1.t0.name: a3-1969.1.t2.eleven_v3
a3-1969.1.t0.text: After inflation, the 1969 retiree averaged 5 .6 % a year.

a3-1928.1.t0.name: a3-1928.1.t2.eleven_v3
a3-1928.1.t0.text: Yet, 1928 ended with $1 .21 million in 1928 dollars and 1969 ran out of money in its 28th year.

a3-share.1.t0.name: a3-share.1.t1.eleven_v3
a3-share.1.t0.text: What the four failures share is their first decade.

a3-decade.1.t0.name: a3-decade.1.t2.eleven_v3
a3-decade.1.t0.text: In every one of them, the portfolio lost money after inflation over its first 10 years.

a3-1966d.1.t0.name: a3-1966d.1.t0.eleven_v3
a3-1966d.1.t0.text: After inflation, the first decade of the 1966 retiree averaged minus 1 .8%.

a3-mirror-d.1.t0.name: a3-mirror-d.1.t0.eleven_v3
a3-mirror-d.1.t0.text: In the first decade, the mirror retiree averaged 6 .9 % a year after inflation.

a3-nuance.1.t0.name: a3-nuance.1.t0.eleven_v3
a3-nuance.1.t0.text: To be precise, across all 69 start years, the 30 -year real return still lines up best with how much is left at the end.

a3-nuance.2.t0.name: a3-nuance.2.t0.eleven_v3
a3-nuance.2.t0.text: But every retiree who ran out, met a bad first decade.

a3-avg-callback.1.t0.name: a3-avg-callback.1.t1.eleven_v3
a3-avg-callback.1.t0.text: The 9 .7 % average described the 1966 retiree perfectly, and it said nothing about 1991.

a3-limits.1.t0.name: a3-limits.1.t2.eleven_multilingual_v2
a3-limits.1.t0.text: Now the limits of this analysis.

a3-limits.2.t0.name: a3-limits.2.t0.eleven_v3
a3-limits.2.t0.text: This is history, not a forecast.

a3-usonly.1.t0.name: a3-usonly.1.t0.eleven_v3
a3-usonly.1.t0.text: It is U .S. only, one country with one set of markets.

a3-overlap.1.t0.name: a3-overlap.1.t1.eleven_v3
a3-overlap.1.t0.text: The 69 windows overlap, so 98 years of data hold only three separate 30 -year stretches.

a3-bare.1.t0.name: a3-bare.1.t0.eleven_v3
a3-bare.1.t0.text: And the model is bare, no taxes, no fees, one portfolio mix, and one withdrawal rule.

a3-bare.2.t0.name: a3-bare.2.t1.eleven_v3
a3-bare.2.t0.text: Change any of those, and every number here changes too.

method.1.t0.name: method.1.t0.eleven_v3
method.1.t0.text: The data, annual returns compiled at NYU Stern, and consumer prices from the Bureau of Labor Statistics via FRED.

method-model.1.t0.name: method-model.1.t0.eleven_v3
method-model.1.t0.text: Returns include dividends and bond coupons, and the portfolio is rebalanced once a year.

method-model.2.t0.name: method-model.2.t2.eleven_multilingual_v2
method-model.2.t0.text: Every number and formula is listed in the description.

outro.1.t0.name: outro.1.t0.eleven_v3
outro.1.t0.text: Two retirees, one average, and a fate decided by the order of the years.
